audit.reasoning: Quote: we held no file; I downloaded the cited Waikato thesis (open, hdl 10289/5755), scanned the cited pages, and the deciding sentence is verbatim on p.51 sec 3.3, with pp.53-54 reinforcing strict initial stress (prefixes take the stress; non-phonemic). Deciding source is a 2010 MA-thesis grammar sketch, the top Glottolog item, fieldwork-based but impressionistic and register-blind. Web search found the one dedicated prosodic study, Heinz 2004 (UCLA MA thesis, open), now downloaded: it confirms initial main stress for the Normal (everyday spoken) register ('main stress always falls on the initial syllable', p.31) but describes the Citation register as penult-plus-alternating-leftward with main stress on the leftmost stressed syllable and CVV syllables attracting stress (pp.13-15), i.e. odd-parity all-light words would carry main stress on the second syllable in careful/citation speech. sources.quote: 'the data in this project demonstrates a fixed stress pattern where primary stress falls on the initial syllable for bisyllabic words (3.38), as it does for trisyllabic words (3.39), and even for those of four syllables or more (3.40)' (p.51); suffixation leaves stress on root, prefixation shifts stress to the prefix 'to maintain the initial position' (p.53); 'Stress is not phonemic in Kwaraqae, and not all words carry stress' (p.53).

sources.citation: Heinz, Jeffrey N. 2004. CV Metathesis in Kwara'ae. MA thesis, UCLA. 122 pp.
sources.quote: Normal register: 'Unlike the Citation form, in the Normal form, main stress always falls on the initial syllable' (p.31); 'Main stress is on the initial syllable, and heavy syllables bear stress, except when following an initial light syllable' (p.32). Citation register: 'Stress in the Citation form is rhythmic; generally, secondary stress falls on the penultimate and alternating syllables leftward. Main stress falls on the leftmost stressed syllable'; 'If the final syllable is CVV ... it receives stress, as do alternating syllables to its left' (pp.13-14). Stress cued by intensity/loudness, n
sources.locator: sec 2.1.5 pp.13-15 (Citation form); sec 2.2.4 p.31 and Normal-register summary p.32; sec 2.4 pp.37-38
sources.note: Only dedicated phonological study of Kwara'ae prosody; splits stress by register (Normal: initial main stress; Citation: penult-plus-alternating with main stress leftmost, CVV attracts stress) which Macdonald's 3-page section does not; should be added as second source and the register caveat noted.

sources.citation: Heinz, Jeffrey. 2005. Reconsidering Linearity: Evidence from CV Metathesis. Proceedings of WCCFL 24, 200-208. Cascadilla.
sources.quote: 'In the Normal form, almost every stressed syllable is heavy' (Stress-to-Weight); Kwara'ae treated as trochaic; 'the Normal form of Kwara'ae ... differs from the Citation form stress pattern (itself predictable)'; defers stress details to Heinz (2004).
sources.locator: sec 3.1 p.202; sec 3.4 p.204 and fn.12
sources.note: Published peer-reviewed companion to Heinz 2004; states Normal vs Citation stress patterns differ and that stressed syllables are heavy in Normal form; citable published anchor for the register split.

tone.summary: No tone statement; prosody described purely as predictable stress (Normal register: initial main stress; Citation register: penult-alternating rhythm with leftmost main stress, CVV/long vowels attract stress).

tone.summary: No tone statement; word stress normally initial, moved to the final syllable of the last word of a focused phrase (phrasal stress).

tone.summary: OT paper on foot structure and citation vs. discourse registers of Rotuman and Kwara'ae ('register' = speech style, not pitch). All 15 pages searched: nothing on tone, pitch or accent-as-pitch. States trochaic feet, primary stress in a right-edge foot and secondary feet at the left edge in Kwara'ae.
